newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - AmEx president pleased with card trend.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - AmEx president pleased with card trend.

text.p: Kenneth Chenault, named to the number-two job at financial services giant American Express Co Wednesday, said he is encouraged by stablization of the company's charge card business and excited about growth opportunities.

"We have had declining share (in U.S. charge cards) this decade," he said in a telephone interview. "I'm encouraged that we have reversed that trend. We did not lose share in 1996 for the first time in a decade."

Chenault, an American Express employee since 1981, was named president and chief operating officer. Moreover, chairman and chief executive Harvey Golub, said in a letter to employees that the elevation recognizes Chenault as the second-ranking executive and also makes him the "primary internal candidate" to eventually take the top spot. But Golub said he plans to stay another seven years and then retire when he turns 65.
The president's job has been vacant since Jeffrey Stiefler left the comany in September, 1995.
Chenault, a 45-year-old black American, has been the American Express executive most closely identified with the revitalization of the company's card business.

Alfred Edmond jr, vice president and executive editor of Black Enterprise Magazine, said the "conventional wisdom is that if anybody is poised to break the barrier" to a black American becoming chief executive of a major U.S. multinational corporation, it is Chenault. He said Chenault and a small group of other black American executives are "testing how high the glass ceiling really is."

Asked how he felt about the chance to become chief executive, Chenault said he preferred to focus on the job at hand. "The only thing I can control is my performance and that's what I'm focused on," he said.

Chenault said growth areas he is most excited about include the corporate card and small business card products. He also said the campaign to forge partnerships outside the U.S. has been very successful. In those arrangements, the partners issue charge or credit cards on the AmEx merchant network.

Asked about American Express's campaign to persuade the U.S. Visa and MasterCard associations to let their member banks issue American Express cards, Chenault said he was not in a position to know details of or comment on a U.S. Justice Department probe of competitive practices in the industry. But he added, "I think from a fairness standpoint it's really hard to argue with freedom of choice." He said consumers will benefit by having more choices if the banks can issue not only Visa cards and MasterCards but American Express cards too.

The card associations have argued that the present system which has American Express, Visa, MasterCard and Dean Witter Discover & Co all vying with their own systems is a more competitive environment.
Golub's letter said three other top executives, Chuck Farr, Richard Goeltz, and Jon Linen, will continue in their duties although Farr and Linen will now report to Chenault.

Golub said all of the businesses except for the American Express Bank and Financial Advisors will report to Chenault immediately. After an unspecified transition period, the bank and Financial Advisors will also report to Chenault.
